deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Riemann writes xi(t) = Pi(s/2)(s-1) pi^{-s/2} zeta(s) with s = 1/2 + t i (next page). The alpha_nu are the positive roots of xi(t)=0. He introduces a smooth counting function lambda with lambda(alpha_n) = n. The page has two parts.

PART A. Asymptotic expansion of the zero-counting function from the product for xi, using Euler-Maclaurin summation over the zeros.

(A1) Replace t by -i t, so s = 1/2 + t with t real and large. Then log xi(-it) - log xi(0) = Sum_nu log(1 + t^2/alpha_nu^2). This gives
Sum log(1+t^2/alpha^2) = log Pi(t/2+1/4) + log(t-1/2) - (t/2+1/4) log pi + log zeta(1/2+t) - log xi(0).

(A2) The zeta term decays exponentially. By Stirling [my fill-in: (z+1/2) log z - z + (1/2) log 2pi with z = t/2+1/4] this becomes
(t/2+7/4) log(t/2pi) - t/2 + 2 log pi + (3/2) log 2 - log xi(0) + a_1/t + a_2/t^2 + ...

(A3) Euler-Maclaurin, with nu treated as a continuous variable through x = alpha, d nu = lambda'(x) dx, and d/d nu = (1/lambda') d/dx:
-Sum_{nu>=n} f(alpha_nu) = [ F(x) - f/2 + (1/12) f'/lambda' - (1/720)(1/lambda') d/dx((1/lambda') d/dx(f'/lambda')) + ... ] at x = alpha_n,
where F' = f lambda'.

(A4) Apply this with f = log(1+t^2/x^2), splitting off the first n-1 zeros:
Sum = Sum_{nu=1}^{n-1} log(1+t^2/alpha_nu^2) + Int_{alpha_n}^oo log(1+t^2/x^2) lambda'(x) dx + (1/2) log(1+t^2/alpha_n^2) - (1/12) f'(alpha_n)/lambda'(alpha_n) + ...
For large t, log(1+t^2/alpha^2) = 2 log t - 2 log alpha + alpha^2/t^2 - ... Hence the log t part of the discrete terms is (2n-1) log t - 2 Sum_1^{n-1} log alpha_nu - log alpha_n + Int_{alpha}^oo ...

(A5) Main term of lambda': (1/2pi) log(x/2pi). Substitute x = t y:
Int_0^oo log(1+t^2/x^2)(1/2pi) log(x/2pi) dx = (t/2pi) Int_0^oo log(1+1/y^2)(log y + log(t/2pi)) dy.
The two needed integrals come from a Beta integral.
- Substituting z = 1/(1+y): Int_0^oo (1+y)^mu y^nu dy = Int_0^1 (1-z)^nu z^{-2-mu-nu} dz = Pi(nu) Pi(-2-mu-nu)/Pi(-1-mu).
- This equals 2 Int (1+y^2)^mu y^{2nu+1} dy = 2 Int (1+1/y^2)^mu y^{2mu+2nu+1} dy.
- With nu = beta - mu - 1/2: 2 Int (1+1/y^2)^mu y^{2beta} dy = Pi(-3/2-beta) Pi(beta-mu-1/2)/Pi(-1-mu).
- Differentiate in mu at mu = 0. Since 1/Pi(-1) = 0 and Psi(-1-mu)/Pi(-1-mu) -> -1, this gives 2 Int log(1+1/y^2) y^{2beta} dy = -Pi(-3/2-beta) Pi(beta-1/2).
- At beta = 0 this is -Pi(-3/2)Pi(-1/2) = 2pi.
- Differentiating once more in beta: -Pi(-3/2)Pi(-1/2)(Psi(-1/2) - Psi(-3/2)) = -4pi.
- Result: Int_0^oo log(1+1/y^2) dy = -Int_0^oo log y log(1+1/y^2) dy = pi.
So the main integral equals (t/2) log(t/2pi) - t/2, exactly reproducing the leading terms of (A2).

(A6) Correction terms x^{-2m} in lambda'. Integrate by parts:
Int_alpha^oo log(1+t^2/x^2) x^{-2m} dx = alpha^{1-2m} log(1+t^2/alpha^2)/(2m-1) - (2t^2/(2m-1)) Int_alpha^oo dx/(x^{2m}(t^2+x^2)).
Expand 1/(1+x^2/t^2) geometrically up to the remainder. The only part not expandable in powers of alpha is
-(2/(2m-1)) (-1)^m t^{1-2m} Int_{alpha/t}^oo dy/(1+y^2), which tends to -(pi/(2m-1)) (-1)^m / t^{2m-1}.
Matching with a_{2m-1}/t^{2m-1} gives
lambda'(x) = (1/2pi) log(x/2pi) - Sum ((2m-1)/pi)(-1)^m a_{2m-1}/x^{2m}.

(A7) Match the coefficient of log t (7/4 from A2) against the Euler-Maclaurin side:
7/4 = (2n-1) - 2(lambda(alpha_n) - C) = 2C - 1, so C = 11/8. Hence
lambda(x) = (x/2pi) log(x/2pi) - x/2pi + 11/8 + Sum (-1)^m a_{2m-1}/(pi x^{2m-1}).

Interpretation (mine). Since lambda(alpha_n) = n means the smooth count at the nth zero is n - 1/2, lambda = N_smooth + 1/2. This gives N_smooth(T) = T/2pi log(T/2pi) - T/2pi + 7/8 + ..., i.e. lambda = theta(T)/pi + 3/2. From Stirling, a_1 = -1/48, so the next term is +1/(48 pi T). This is exactly the smooth part of the Riemann-von Mangoldt formula, derived heuristically (S(T) is ignored).

PART B. Saddle-point treatment of the theta/Mellin integral Int_0^oo e^{-n^2 pi x} x^{s/2-1} dx with s = 1/2 + t i.

(B1) The exponent is -n^2 pi x + (ti/2 - 3/4) log x. The saddle point is at x = ti/(2 n^2 pi).

(B2) Put n + beta = sqrt(t/2pi), so that ti/2 = pi i (n+beta)^2 and the saddle point is near x = i. Set x = i + y with y = z sqrt(2pi/t) i, i.e. x = i(1 + z sqrt(2pi/t)). Then log(i+y) = pi i/2 + log(1 - y i).

(B3) First version, in y:
- Exponent: -n^2 pi i - n^2 pi y - (pi^2/2)(n+beta)^2 + pi y (n+beta)^2 + ...
- The linear terms combine to e^{pi y (2 n beta + beta^2)}.

(B4) In z, with n^2 = t/2pi - 2beta sqrt(t/2pi) + beta^2 and log(1+w) = w - w^2/2 + w^3/3:
- The large linear terms cancel.
- The integrand becomes e^{-n^2 pi i} (1 + z sqrt(2pi/t))^{-3/4} exp(2 pi i beta z - pi i z^2/2 - pi i z beta^2 sqrt(2pi/t) + pi i z^3/3 sqrt(2pi/t) + ...).
- That is a Gaussian (Fresnel) kernel in z with corrections in powers of sqrt(2pi/t).
This is the germ of the Riemann-Siegel asymptotic expansion around N = floor(sqrt(t/2pi)).
errors: No substantive errors found in the main computations: the Stirling constant terms, the 7/4, the Beta-integral manipulations, the Euler-Maclaurin coefficients (1/2, 1/12, 1/720), the integration by parts, the constant 11/8 and the cubic saddle-point expansion all check.

Side note '-Psi(-mu) = 1/mu - Psi(1-mu)' does not match the functional equation Psi(x) = 1/x + Psi(x-1); the correct relation is Psi(-1-mu) = Psi(-mu) + 1/mu. Either a slip or a misreading; it does not affect the result, since the needed limit Psi(-1-mu)/Pi(-1-mu) -> -1 is used correctly.

Part A is heuristic: Euler-Maclaurin over zeros presupposes a smooth interpolating lambda with lambda(alpha_n) = n exactly. This ignores the fluctuating term S(T), so it determines only the smooth part of the counting function.
In (A4) the second integral is written with lower limit alpha rather than alpha_n and with f'(alpha) unspecified; these are notational.

results.what: Asymptotic expansion of log xi on the real s-axis: Sum log(1+t^2/alpha^2) = (t/2+7/4)log(t/2pi) - t/2 + 2log pi + (3/2)log 2 - log xi(0) + O(1/t)
results.modern_name: Stirling asymptotics of the completed zeta function / Hadamard product

results.what: Euler-Maclaurin summation over zeros indexed by a smooth counting function lambda(alpha_n) = n
Int_0^oo log(1+1/y^2) dy = pi and Int_0^oo log y log(1+1/y^2) dy = -pi, via differentiation of a Beta integral
results.modern_name: Beta-function / Feynman differentiation under integral sign

results.what: Smooth counting function lambda(x) = x/2pi log(x/2pi) - x/2pi + 11/8 + Sum (-1)^m a_{2m-1}/(pi x^{2m-1}), equivalently N_smooth(T) = T/2pi log(T/2pi) - T/2pi + 7/8 + 1/(48 pi T) + ... = theta(T)/pi + 1
results.modern_name: Riemann-von Mangoldt formula, smooth part with constant 7/8 (theta(T)/pi + 1)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1859 (leading terms, stated); von Mangoldt 1895/1905 (proof, with 7/8 term); Backlund 1914-18 (explicit)

results.what: Saddle-point expansion of Int e^{-n^2 pi x} x^{s/2-1} dx near x = i with n + beta = sqrt(t/2pi), producing exp(2 pi i beta z - pi i z^2/2 + O(t^{-1/2}))
results.modern_name: Saddle-point (stationary phase) step underlying the Riemann-Siegel formula

deep.surprise_reason: The Riemann-Siegel saddle-point work is known to be Riemann's through Siegel (1932). The less familiar item is Part A, a heuristic Euler-Maclaurin derivation of the smooth zero-counting function. It includes the constant 11/8 (equivalently 7/8 in N(T)) and the inverse-power corrections, i.e. theta(T)/pi + 1, which are usually attributed to von Mangoldt and Backlund. Riemann's 1859 paper only states the leading terms. Because the derivation is heuristic and parts of the Nachlass have been surveyed (Siegel, Edwards), I am unsure whether it has been noted; it is a notable but not major unpublished detail.
